rationale: The book’s core identification—lamp oil as inwardly retained, Spirit-produced obedience that can later shine in visible conduct—explains the combined evidence better than the conventional identification of the oil with the Holy Spirit himself. Proverbs 6:23 supplies the controlling lamp/light framework: commandment, light, and corrective instruction belong together. Psalm 141:5 associates received reproof with oil; Proverbs 21:20 conspicuously joins wisdom, stored oil, and the fool’s depletion; Proverbs 7:1-3, Psalm 119:11, Jeremiah 31:33, and 1 John 2:4 distinguish possessing commandments outwardly from having their truth inwardly. Matthew’s wise/fool contrast elsewhere turns on hearing and doing, while Matthew 5:16 connects shining light with visible works. This also fits the oil’s personal accumulation, exhaustion, non-transferability, and need to be acquired before the crisis. By contrast, the Holy Spirit is given rather than purchased, is not depleted by being shared, and can be received suddenly. The distinction between lamp oil and compounded anointing oil further weakens the usual transfer from anointing texts. Some of the book’s elaborations exceed what the evidence securely establishes, but its central interpretation is stronger than the available alternatives.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The oil represents persevering, Spirit-enabled discipleship or practical good works in a broad sense, without specifically denoting inwardly stored truth, accepted correction, or ‘pressed’ and tested obedience. On this reading, the parable contrasts disciples whose conduct has prepared them for final judgment with nominal disciples whose profession lacks enduring works; the oil is the practical provision that keeps their witness burning.
counter_case: Matthew 5:16 directly associates shining light with good works, making faithful conduct the closest explicit Matthean correlate.
Matthew 7:24-27 defines wise and foolish hearers by whether they do Jesus’ sayings, supporting obedience without requiring each component of the lamp scene to have a separate fixed referent.
Matthew 25:31-46 places deeds of mercy in the same judgment discourse, strengthening a broad works-oriented reading.
The purchasing, storage, and shortage of oil can function as ordinary narrative imagery for preparedness; they need not encode truth, reproof, inward law, and lifelong testing separately.

Psalm 141:5 calls reproof ‘excellent oil’ in a comparison involving the head, not explicitly lamp fuel, while Proverbs 21:20 may simply praise prudent household storage. Their use as precise symbolic definitions is therefore disputable.
book_explanatory_advantages: It distinguishes lamp oil from anointing oil using Exodus 25:6, 27:20, and 30:22-33, directly answering a major premise of the Holy-Spirit reading.
It explains why the oil is accumulated beforehand, privately retained, exhaustible, and non-transferable: another person’s formed obedience cannot be lent at the final hour.
It integrates the exact cluster of wise/foolish, stored oil, and depletion in Proverbs 21:20 with Matthew 25.
It gives differentiated roles to lamp, oil, and light: the commandment possessed, its truth and correction internalized into obedience, and that obedience made visible.
It relates Proverbs 6:23 and Psalm 141:5 into a coherent sequence of commandment, correction, life, and illumination.
It accounts for the repeated inward-storage texts—Psalm 119:11, Proverbs 7:1-3, Jeremiah 31:33—and for 1 John 2:4’s contrast between profession and truth actually present within.
It preserves Ezekiel 36:27 and Zechariah 4 by treating the Spirit as the divine cause of obedient work rather than automatically equating the lamp’s oil with the Spirit himself.
It fits the broader biblical definition of wisdom as hearing and doing, which is especially relevant because Matthew explicitly calls the two groups wise and foolish.
counter_explanatory_advantages: A broad ‘faithful deeds’ interpretation is simpler and rests more directly on Matthew’s own language about wise doers and visible good works.
It avoids treating every occurrence of oil, buying, storage, pressing, or inwardness as part of a uniform symbolic code.
It does not depend on transferring Psalm 141:5’s head-oil simile or Proverbs 21:20’s household inventory into a technical definition of lamp oil.
It can retain the parable’s primary emphasis on readiness for judgment without over-specifying the psychological process by which obedience is formed.
unresolved_objections: The evidence supports inwardly formed obedience more securely than every phrase of the entry; ‘tested, pressed fruit’ is evocative but depends partly on olive pressing and Gethsemane associations rather than an explicit interpretive key.
Psalm 141:5 may concern soothing or honorific head oil rather than lamp fuel, so its connection to the virgins’ oil remains analogical.
Proverbs 21:20 can be read literally as prudent storage contrasted with wastefulness; its verbal overlap with Matthew is suggestive but not conclusive.
The book’s rule that symbolic meanings hold uniformly across Scripture is too strong in principle because imagery can vary by genre and context.
The Holy Spirit reading remains plausible at the broader theological level, especially through Zechariah 4, even though it handles the parable’s finite and purchasable oil less naturally.
The simpler good-works interpretation comes close to the book’s position and may capture the parable’s main thrust without validating all of the book’s finer distinctions.
